title: How to Create a Quotation Before an Invoice
summary: Learn how to create a quotation before an invoice, including essential details, pricing, taxes, payment terms, and steps for accurate business billing.
body_markdown:
# **How to Create a Quotation Before an Invoice**


To make an invoice make sense, you should prepare a quotation first. It helps a business share the expected costs, the actual work or product scope and get a green light from the customer before anything truly starts. At the same time, it sets a calm baseline between buyer and seller, so later there are fewer surprises, like payment terms, final totals , or what exactly is included.


*A good quote for small businesses, freelancers, and anyone who services others is also more professional, and the billing process is typically much easier as well, you know, less back and forth. So in this blog, we will guide you on* ***how to create a quotation before an invoice*** *.*


## **What do you mean by a Quotation?**


It is a formal document that will demonstrate the estimated or agreed-upon cost of the products or services you are proposing to supply to a customer, and it will generally include information on the name of the item, the quantity, taxes if applicable, any possible discounts, and the terms of payment.


An invoice is essentially a request for paymet for work that has been performed, whereas a quotation is sent out before the client agrees to the work (either in writing or verbally). If the client is pleased with the quotation and accepts it (both orally and in writing), then you can send an invoice for payment once the work has been performed as agreed.


**To create a Quotation Before an Invoice:**


### ***Include business and customer info***


State the business name, addresses, contracts and registration/legal info required to identify the business, then the customer’s name, address and contact info to identify the customer.


If your business is GST registered in India, you can enter your[GSTIN](https://services.gst.gov.in/services/searchtp) anywhere it's required; this will help ensure the data is correct and make your transition from a quotation to an invoice seamless.


### ***Complete a Unique Quotation Number***


Quotes should be numbered, for example, QT-2026-001, to allow quick retrieval of documents, communicate with the customer and to correlate the approved quote to subsequent invoices. Also add the date of the quotation and also a time frame for the terms and pricing. The term validity is, in essence, the window of time when the pricing and terms apply.


### ***Clearly Describe Products or services***


Include details about each product in sufficient detail for the customer to understand what you are offering so that he or she can accept or reject it. If it’s a service, discuss deliverable project milestones, timelines, etc. – and even what's not in the quoted price – because this helps to avoid disputes later on.


### ***Check pricing, discount and tax calculations***


Calculate the subtotal calculating the quantity by the unit price of each item, then apply any discount that was agreed in the discussion, and apply any taxes (such as GST) as per the appropriate rules.


If the quote is, for instance, for providing ₹10000 worth of services and the tax rate is 18% (GST), then the total quoted amount is ₹11800 before making any other modifications. Always double-check the tax rate and tax treatment before sending; the final invoice should be as per the tax rate applicable to that transaction.


### ***Setup Payment terms and Conditions***


If planned in milestones, explain how payments will be made if an advance payment or deposit is required. Additional information that may be included, such as conditions for cancellation charges to be applied for any additional work done, other important terms, etc., when clearly written, both parties have a clear idea of their roles before the deal progresses.


**Suggested Read:**[International Invoice Formats](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/international-invoice-formats)


### ***Read and deliver the quotation***


Always look at everything before sharing the quotation, including the calculations, customer information, descriptions, and all terms. Save it as a PDF or send it with the accounting system.


Have the customer sign it in writing or confirm it in a clear manner, and then save the accepted quotation for later use when creating the invoice.


## **Conclusion**


Quoting prior to an invoice can help to clarify pricing for businesses, obtain customer approval faster and also ensure that the billing papers are accurate. Usually, the bill is handled smoothly, and very few arguments emerge when the document is complete with all the business information, itemised charges, taxes that apply and payment terms that are easy to follow. Maintaining a consistent quotation-to-invoice process also ensures a smoother financial record keeping process and in general, provides a more professional customer experience from the client's standpoint.

## **FAQS**


### ***What does a quotation include?***


No, a quotation is a price and terms document, whereas an invoice generally requests payment after the business.


### ***Should there be a GST on a quotation?***


It depends, but if there is GST, it ought to display the proper tax approach and a reasonable estimate of the amount of tax.


### ***What is the time period for a quotation?***


The business must establish a reasonable time span of validity, according to the stability of the prices, the project's requirements and the company's commercial conditions.


### ***Which businesses might actually gain from the GST reforms that were proposed?***


Eligible small businesses, manufacturers, exporters and other taxpayers could see advantages from the changes in registration, refunds, compliance procedures and even prosecution provisions, but it really depends on how the final legal framework ends up looking and also on the eligibility terms that are applied. ***en will the recommended GST reforms kick in, basically?***


The effective date can differ for each measure. Businesses should keep track of the official GST Council announcements, CBIC notifications, and the related amendments to understand when every provision becomes applicable, and not just assume it is all at once.
